steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper proposing a federated learning algorithm, inspired by meta-learning, that handles clients with heterogeneous tasks, tested on real-world medical records. Motivate it from on-device data and privacy, explain where standard federated learning and meta-learning fall short, and summarize our method and results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Data on mobile devices: huge value, but can't be centralized
- Federated learning and how it works
- Limitation: heterogeneous datasets / tasks; meta-learning only local
- Our algorithm: loss feedback + partially frozen global model
- Experiments on medical datasets

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Data on mobile devices
  - smartphones, tablets, laptops = primary computing devices; phones indispensable (cite)
  - processors + sensors (cameras, microphones) -> unprecedented amount of data
  - exploiting it to train networks -> much better performance
  - e.g. photos -> better vision model (classify images, segment objects); typed text -> more robust language model for translation
  - but can't gather it: private + very large -> insecure, impossible to store centrally (server)
- Federated learning
  - proposed to address this (cite)
  - clients (devices/locations) send gradients of model params from local training to server, not raw data (cite)
  - server aggregates with weighted average, updates server model, sends updated model back for next iterations
  - shares model params, not data (cite); reduces privacy/security risk, raw data stays on device (cite)
- Limitation
  - works well for homogeneous datasets, much worse for heterogeneous ones with different training tasks
  - real world: client datasets usually heterogeneous, e.g. hospitals' records used to diagnose different diseases
  - meta-learning: exposes models to different tasks to learn new tasks better; handles heterogeneity but devised for local training
- Our algorithm
  - inspired by meta-learning; feed back training loss to server instead of gradients
  - handles heterogeneity across clients, adapts FL to more general applications
  - server (global model) task also differs from all clients
  - freeze half of global model, update other half with local data -> balance global vs local training; better performance, robustness
- Experiments
  - two medical datasets: MIMIC-CXR Database v2.0.0, eICU
  - best over various metrics vs other FL algorithms

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Nowadays smartphones, tablets and laptops are the main computing devices we use, and phones in particular are something many people can't do without. These devices have better and better processors and sensors, like cameras and microphones, and since so many people carry them everywhere they produce an unprecedented amount of data. So if we could use this data effectively and efficiently to train neural networks, the networks would perform much better. For example, the photos from smartphone cameras could be used to train a better computer vision model that classifies different images or segments different objects. And the text people type into their devices could give a more robust language model for translating between languages. But we can't just use all this data together directly. The data from mobile devices is usually private and also very large in quantity, so it is insecure and impossible to collect it all and store it in one centralized location (i.e. a server).

Federated learning was proposed by researchers to deal with these issues. In federated learning, clients (e.g. different devices or locations) train on their local data and send the gradients of all model parameters to the server, instead of sending the original data. The server aggregates the gradients with a weighted average and updates the server model. Then the server sends the updated model to all the clients for the next iterations. So federated learning does not share data, it only shares model parameters. This reduces the privacy and security risks because the raw data stays on the clients' devices.

- Limitation
  - works well for homogeneous datasets, much worse for heterogeneous ones with different training tasks
  - real world: client datasets usually heterogeneous, e.g. hospitals' records used to diagnose different diseases
  - meta-learning: exposes models to different tasks to learn new tasks better; handles heterogeneity but devised for local training
- Our algorithm
  - inspired by meta-learning; feed back training loss to server instead of gradients
  - server (global model) task also differs from all clients
  - freeze half of global model, update other half with local data -> balance global vs local training
- Experiments
  - MIMIC-CXR Database v2.0.0, eICU; best over various metrics vs other FL algorithms

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Nowadays smartphones, tablets and laptops are the main computing devices we use, and phones in particular are something many people can't do without. These devices have better and better processors and sensors, like cameras and microphones, and since so many people carry them everywhere they produce an unprecedented amount of data. So if we could use this data effectively and efficiently to train neural networks, the networks would perform much better. For example, the photos from smartphone cameras could be used to train a better computer vision model that classifies different images or segments different objects. And the text people type into their devices could give a more robust language model for translating between languages. But we can't just use all this data together directly. The data from mobile devices is usually private and also very large in quantity, so it is insecure and impossible to collect it all and store it in one centralized location (i.e. a server).

Federated learning was proposed by researchers to deal with these issues. In federated learning, clients (e.g. different devices or locations) train on their local data and send the gradients of all model parameters to the server, instead of sending the original data. The server aggregates the gradients with a weighted average and updates the server model. Then the server sends the updated model to all the clients for the next iterations. So federated learning does not share data, it only shares model parameters. This reduces the privacy and security risks because the raw data stays on the clients' devices. Federated learning can use data from multiple clients to train the model, but it only works well for homogeneous datasets, and it performs a lot worse for heterogeneous datasets where the training tasks are different. In the real world, though, the datasets from different clients are usually heterogeneous. For example, patients' medical records from different hospitals may be used to diagnose different diseases. Meta-learning, on the other hand, exposes models to different training tasks so they can learn new tasks more productively, so it could handle training on heterogeneous datasets, but it was designed for local data training.

Based on the basic idea of meta-learning, we propose a new federated learning algorithm that sends the training loss back to the server instead of the gradients of the model parameters. This is meant to deal with the heterogeneity of datasets from different clients and to make federated learning work for more general applications. Also, in the heterogeneous training scenario the training task of the server (i.e. the global model) can be different from all of the clients too. To make up for this heterogeneity between the server and the clients, and to further improve the performance and robustness of the algorithm, we freeze half of the global model and only update the other half with local data during federated learning, which balances global training and local training. We run experiments with the proposed algorithm on two medical datasets, MIMIC-CXR Database v2.0.0 and eICU, and it performs the best on various evaluation metrics compared to other federated learning algorithms.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In modern life, smartphones, tablets, and laptops are the primary computing devices, and phones in particular are indispensable for many people [1]. With the development of the processors and sensors of these devices, such as cameras and microphones, an unprecedented amount of data is produced when so many people carry them everywhere. Therefore, if we could exploit such data effectively and efficiently to train neural networks, the performance of the networks would be significantly improved. For instance, with photos from smartphone cameras, we could train a better computer vision model to classify different images or segment different objects. With the text data people enter into their devices, we could obtain a more robust language model to translate different languages. However, directly exploiting these data together is not feasible, because the data from mobile devices are usually private and very large in quantity, which means that it is insecure and impossible to gather all such data together and store it in a centralized location (i.e. a server).

To address these issues, federated learning was proposed [2]. In the framework of federated learning [2], clients (e.g. different devices or locations) transmit the gradients of all model parameters, obtained from training on their local data, to the server instead of the original data. The server then aggregates the gradients with a weighted average and updates the server model, after which it delivers the updated model to all clients for the next iterations. In other words, federated learning does not share data but only shares model parameters [3]. It thus reduces privacy and security risks by keeping the raw data within clients' devices [2]. Although federated learning is capable of using data from multiple clients to train the model, it only works well for homogeneous datasets and performs significantly worse for heterogeneous datasets whose training tasks are different. Yet datasets from different clients are usually heterogeneous in the real world; for example, the medical records of patients from different hospitals may be used to diagnose different diseases. Meta-learning, by contrast, exposes models to different training tasks so that they learn new tasks more productively, and could handle training on heterogeneous datasets, but it is devised for local data training.

Inspired by the basic idea of meta-learning, we propose a novel federated learning algorithm which feeds back the training loss to the server rather than the gradients of model parameters, in order to deal with the heterogeneity of datasets from different clients and adapt federated learning to more general applications. Furthermore, in the heterogeneous training scenario, the training task of the server (i.e. the global model) may also differ from those of all clients. To make up for the heterogeneity between the server and the clients and further enhance the performance and robustness of our algorithm, we freeze half of the global model and update only the other half with local data during federated learning, balancing global and local training. We evaluate the proposed algorithm on two medical datasets, MIMIC-CXR Database v2.0.0 and eICU, where it performs the best over various evaluation metrics compared to other federated learning algorithms.

References:
[1] H. B. McMahan, E. Moore, D. Ramage, S. Hampson, and B. A. y Arcas, “Communication-efficient learning of deep networks from decentralized data,” 2017.
[2] J. Konečný, H. B. McMahan, D. Ramage, and P. Richtárik, “Federated optimization: Distributed machine learning for on-device intelligence,” 2016.
[3] K. Bonawitz, V. Ivanov, B. Kreuter, A. Marcedone, H. B. McMahan, S. Patel, D. Ramage, A. Segal, and K. Seth, “Practical secure aggregation for privacy-preserving machine learning,” in Proceedings of the 2017 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security . ACM, Oct. 2017. [Online]. Available: https://doi.org/10.1145/3133956.3133982
